newsitem.title: UK: LPC - Market calls Yugo debt proposal unacceptable.
newsitem.headline: LPC - Market calls Yugo debt proposal unacceptable.

text.p: LONDON, June 24 (LPC) -- Yugoslavia's proposal to restructure the remainder of its New Financing Agreement (NFA) debt through a syndicated loan is likely to be rejected, syndicated loan and emerging markets specialists said.
"This should be viewed as a first proposal which leaves room for discussion - this is definitely not acceptable in its current form," a banker said.

Yugoslavia has asked for debt forgiveness of 80 percent of its outstanding $2.4 billion debt, and proposes to restructure the remaining $481 million through a 25-year syndicated loan facility, with a nine-year grace period before repayment of principal.

Although International Monetary Fund membership is central to a settlement, a deal could technically be struck which will be activated when Yugoslavia rejoins the IMF, which is not expected before January 1998.

Market sources however believe that the proposal in its current form will be flatly rejected. The debt forgiveness figure of 80 percent is highly contentious, and sources said that figures of 30-50 percent were more realistic.

The structure of the loan was also criticised - although the 25-year maturity was described as just feasible, the nine-year grace period was viewed as aggressive, and sources said that seven years would be more realistic.

The syndicated loan proposal came as a surprise to the loan market as Croatia, Slovenia and Macedonia have opted to restructure debt via Eurobond issues. Some bankers voiced concern over the suitability of a loan, both as a less senior instrument than a Eurobond, and as Yugoslavia's default potential is high.
"Any deal will need to be built on Yugoslavia's debt repayment capacity, which is slight as there is no inflow of capital and the economy is bankrupt," a source commented.

Speculation is rife over the timing of the discussions. The impetus for the resumption of discussions is understood to have come from lenders, which are keen to remove the non-performing loans from their balance sheets and resolve the issue. Chase which is acting as the head of the bank steering committee, was unavailable for comment.

The inflow of funds from Croatia, Slovenia and Macedonia's restructurings have already boosted repayment levels to 60-80 percent of 1988's NFA agreement, which is already a higher repayment figure than was achieved in Poland and Bulgaria's London Club restructurings, and has encouraged banks to adopt a more flexible stance.
Bosnia is expected to reach an agreement with its creditors at the end of this week on the rescheduling of its NFA debt. -- Tessa Walsh LPC Newsroom 44-0171-542-4048
